sections.title: Read this first
sections.text:
A wildcard pack is a prompt writer. The same pack can render tags for an anime model or sentences for a prose model, but only if you build it with the target family in mind. Most of the work is in three choices: the dialect (tags or sentences), the order of the parts, and whether the model uses a negative at all.
Model popularity below was gathered on 2026-10-15 from ComfyUI's official template usage, Civitai ecosystem counts and one Hugging Face download report. Civitai and Hugging Face couldn't be read directly, so the numbers are rough. This field moves fast: recheck them before you rely on them.
Rank | Family | Why | Depth here
1 | Illustrious XL (v0.1 to v3.5, and merges) | The largest LoRA ecosystem on Civitai (201K+) | In depth
2 | Pony Diffusion V6 (V7 on AuraFlow) | 103K+ models, 2.37B+ images on Civitai | In depth
3 | Flux.1 and Flux.2 (Dev, Klein) | 23 official ComfyUI templates, many LoRAs | In depth
4 | Z-Image Turbo and Base | The second most opened single ComfyUI template | In depth
5 | Qwen-Image and Qwen-Image 2.1 (and Edit) | The most opened open-weights template family | In depth
6 | NoobAI-XL (eps and v-pred) | 8K+ resources, the strongest Danbooru coverage | In depth
7 | Wan 2.2 (video) | 12K+ template opens | In depth
8 | SDXL base and realistic SDXL fine-tunes | 2.27M Hugging Face downloads a month | Short
9 | Krea 2 | 10.6K template opens, released June 2026 | Short
10 | LTX-2.x (video) | 26K template opens across versions | Short
11 | Anima | New and small (733 template opens) but rising among anime users | In depth
12 | SD 1.5 | About 1.6M Hugging Face downloads a month, a legacy LoRA base | Short
13 | Chroma, SD 3.5, HiDream, Animagine, Kolors, Neta Lumina, HunyuanImage, Playground, PixArt, Stable Cascade | Little data | One table row each
For your pack: decide your target family before you write options. Tag models want options like "red dress"; prose models want "a flowing red silk dress". If you serve both, keep options as short phrases and let the template and the model header do the rest.

sections.title: How the text encoder reads your prompt
sections.text:
Chunks
CLIP models read 75 tokens at a time. A longer prompt is cut into 75-token chunks that are encoded apart and joined. Attributes that land in different chunks bind loosely, so a long tag prompt quietly loses structure. 40 to 70 tags is already two or three chunks; most good Illustrious prompts are 20 to 40 tags. T5 and LLM encoders don't chunk.
Early words
Every family gives early words more weight. Put the subject first.
BREAK
In A1111 and Forge, BREAK starts a new chunk, which keeps one subject's tags together. It is not core ComfyUI syntax: the plain CLIP Text Encode node treats it as a word. Some node packs support it; the core way is two encodes joined with Conditioning (Concat). It means nothing to T5 or LLM encoders.
Weights
"(word:1.2)" raises a word, "(word:0.8)" lowers it. ComfyUI blends weighted words against an empty prompt, so the same number can feel different from A1111. 1.05 to 1.4 is the useful range; above 1.5 it tends to burn. Qwen-Image, Z-Image and Flux.2 switch weights off, so the brackets reach the model as text. Escape real parentheses: "name \(series\)".
Binding
Models mix up which words go with which noun. Write each colour next to its noun ("red dress"; on tag models the compound tag), use two or three colours per image, and never repeat a tag: a duplicate acts like an uncontrolled weight.
LoRA triggers
A trigger word wakes a LoRA. Take it from the model page and keep it exactly as written. Start at strength 0.7 to 0.8; stack two or three at 0.4 to 0.8 each, under about 2 in total. A LoRA only works on the base family it was trained for.
Embeddings
"embedding:name" (or "(embedding:name:1.2)") in the text. Like LoRAs, they belong to one family. Negative embeddings such as EasyNegative go in a negative.
Family | Text encoder | Length | 75-token chunks | Weights
SD 1.5 | CLIP ViT-L | 75 tokens a chunk | yes | yes
SDXL, Pony V6, Illustrious, NoobAI, Animagine | CLIP ViT-L + OpenCLIP bigG | 75 tokens a chunk | yes | yes
Flux.1, SD 3.5, Chroma | T5-XXL (with CLIP on Flux.1 and SD 3.5) | long (Flux.1 up to 512 tokens) | no | parsed, weak
HiDream | CLIP + T5 + Llama 3.1 | about 128 tokens | no | parsed, untested
Flux.2 | Mistral-family LLM | long | no | off (literal text)
Qwen-Image | Qwen2.5-VL | long, keep under 200 words | no | off (literal text)
Z-Image | Qwen3-4B | long | no | off (literal text)
Anima | Qwen3 0.6B | long | no | untested
Wan 2.x | umT5-XXL | 512 tokens | no | parsed, untested
For your pack:
- Keep weight brackets out of option text in a pack meant for several families. Write emphasis in words, or weight in a family-specific fixed value.
- On CLIP models, a whole prompt of 20 to 40 tags fits the budget. Use the variation budget below to keep it there.
- Put a LoRA's trigger inside the option that stands for the LoRA, so they always come together. Never let the Cleaner's blocklist or fuzzy dedupe touch trigger words.

sections.title: Negatives and CFG
sections.text:
A negative prompt only works when the sampler runs real classifier-free guidance, which means CFG above 1. Distilled and few-step models run at CFG 1, where the negative is not used at all.
Family | Negative used? | Settings | Notes
SD 1.5, SDXL, Pony, Illustrious, NoobAI, Animagine | yes | CFG about 4 to 7 | Short standing negative plus option negatives.
Flux.1 dev and schnell | no | CFG 1; Flux guidance (about 3.5) is a different knob | Use positive wording, or NAG.
Flux.2 (Dev, Klein) | no | no negative prompt | Use positive wording.
Z-Image Turbo | no | guidance 0 to 2 | Put exclusions in positive wording or constraints.
Z-Image Base | yes | CFG 3 to 5 |
Qwen-Image, Qwen-Image 2.1 | yes, at true CFG above 1 | true_cfg 4; the default negative is a single space | Lightning setups at CFG 1 ignore it.
Anima Base / Turbo | yes / no | CFG 4 to 5 / CFG 1 |
Chroma | yes | guidance about 3 | De-distilled, so real negatives work.
HiDream Full / Dev and Fast | yes / no | CFG about 5 / CFG 1 |
SD 3.5 Large and Medium / Large Turbo | yes / no | CFG 3.5 to 7 / guidance 0 to 1 |
Wan 2.2 | yes at CFG above 1 | 4 to 8 step accelerated setups run CFG 1 | Then the anti-stillness negative does nothing.
Kolors, Playground v2.5, HunyuanImage 2.1 | yes | CFG about 3 to 6.5 |
Lightning, Hyper, LCM, Turbo variants | no at CFG 1 | CFG-preserving Hyper variants run CFG 5 to 8; SDXL Flash 2.5 to 3.5 | Check the variant's card.
Krea 2 | not documented | Raw and 8-step Turbo | Test it; assume Turbo ignores it.
Negatives work best on a concept the prompt actually invites ("hat" when the outfit tends to bring one). A long generic negative dilutes itself and can cancel things you asked for. To move the camera, say it in the prompt: a negative is not a composition tool. The built-in NAGuidance node brings negatives back on some distilled models.
For your pack:
- Every pack feature that relies on negatives (option negatives, $negatives, a safe guard, the negative template) needs CFG above 1. Say so in the pack's description.
- For CFG 1 models, put exclusions into positive wording ("an empty street", "plain background") and into constraints.
- Option negatives follow usage: they reach the negative output only when the template renders that variable. That is the right home for a word one option invites.

sections.title: Illustrious XL
sections.text:
An SDXL fine-tune by OnomaAI, trained on Danbooru images with Danbooru tags. It is the default choice for anime characters without a LoRA, because it knows thousands of characters by their tag. v2.0 handles 512 to 1536 px and reads short sentences better; v3.5 is a v-prediction model.
Prompt form
Danbooru tags, comma separated, with spaces instead of underscores ("long hair", not long_hair). Parentheses are weight syntax, so escape them in names: "name \(series\)". Characters work by tag ("hatsune miku, vocaloid"). Matching canon colours reinforce a character; contradicting them makes the two fight.
Order
Quality, count (1girl, solo), character, series, artist, appearance, outfit, pose, expression, setting, light, camera, style. NoobAI's template (below) is the order the whole family follows.
Quality tags
"masterpiece, best quality, amazing quality, very aesthetic, absurdres", or the shorter "masterpiece, best quality, absurdres". These are community habits, not an OnomaAI spec. Some merges repeat them at the end.
Rating
Danbooru rating words (general, sensitive, questionable, explicit) or the merge's own form. Read the merge's page.
Negative
"worst quality, low quality, lowres, bad anatomy, bad hands, extra digits, jpeg artifacts, signature, watermark, username". For more push, weight a tag ("(bad hands:1.2)") instead of repeating it.
Settings
Euler a or DPM++ 2M, CFG about 4 to 7, 20 to 30 steps, SDXL sizes (1024×1024, 832×1216, 1216×832). v-pred versions need v-pred sampling settings.
Mistakes
Pony score tags (they do nothing here); five artist tags at once (the styles mush together); tags renamed on Danbooru after the model was trained; 60 or more tags; a colour on its own ("red, dress") instead of next to its noun ("red dress").
For your pack:
- Write options as tags. Keep a whole prompt at 20 to 40 tags, which is one or two 75-token chunks.
- Put the count tag first in the template, before $character.
- Keep the quality header in a fixed value, or in the model header derivation from Recommended pack structure.
- Prefer one named outfit ("school uniform", "sundress") per option to a pile of garment tags.
- Give each colour its noun inside the option ("red dress", "blue eyes") and keep two or three colours per image.

sections.title: Pony Diffusion V6 XL
sections.text:
An SDXL fine-tune trained on about 2.6M images, balanced across anime, cartoon, furry and pony sources and across safe, questionable and explicit ratings. Artist names were removed from training. About half the images had natural-language captions, so short sentences work, but tags are more reliable for specifics.
Score string
Start every prompt with the full string "score_9, score_8_up, score_7_up, score_6_up, score_5_up, score_4_up". The model card says a bare score_9 is much weaker. Never invent scores like score_9.5.
Source tags
source_anime, source_cartoon, source_furry, source_pony, right after the scores. They steer the style. For human anime, put "source_furry, source_pony" in the negative.
Rating tags
rating_safe, rating_questionable, rating_explicit, after the source tag. Exactly one per prompt.
Order
Scores, source, rating, count, character, appearance, outfit, pose, expression, setting, light and camera, style.
Settings
Clip skip 2 (CLIP Set Last Layer at -2 in ComfyUI). Without it you get low-quality blobs.
Negative
Not needed for good results. Common additions: "score_4, score_5, score_6, source_furry, source_pony, watermark, signature, artist name". It sometimes draws fake signatures that negatives can't fully remove.
Realism
V6 itself is weak at photos. Realism comes from merges and LoRAs, which often want their own tags (such as a photo source tag). Follow the merge's page. For safe images on a mixed merge, put rating_safe in the prompt and rating_explicit in the negative.
Pony V7
Built on AuraFlow, so Model Info reads it as auraflow. Treat it as a sentence model with an optional tag tail: special tags, then a plain description of the subject, then style, then extra tags. Its special tags are much weaker than V6's, so don't reuse the V6 score string.
Mistakes
A shortened score string; score tags in the middle; artist names; clip skip 1; Pony LoRAs on an Illustrious checkpoint (different bases, they don't transfer cleanly).
For your pack:
- The score string is a constant: a fixed value, or the pony branch of the model header derivation.
- Make the rating tag come from a $rating driver so it never disagrees with the outfit and pose (see Adult (NSFW) packs).
- A source tag can be a small wildcard that a style driver constrains, so "source_anime" and "source_cartoon" never mix.
- Model Info detects V6 by "pony" or "pdxl" in the file name. Name your merges that way, or add a variant rule.

sections.title: NoobAI-XL
sections.text:
An Illustrious-based model by Laxhar, trained on Danbooru and e621. It comes in eps and v-prediction versions. Its card gives the most explicit tag order in the anime family.
Template
"<1girl/1boy/1other>, <character>, <series>, <artists>, <special tags>, <general tags>, <other tags>". Special tags are quality, aesthetic and date.
Quality tags
Ranked by percentile: masterpiece above the 95th, best quality 85 to 95, good quality 60 to 85, normal quality 30 to 60, worst quality 30 and below. "very awa" is the top 5% by aesthetic score; "worst aesthetic" the bottom 5%.
Date tags
"year 2021", or a period: newest (2021 to 2024), recent, mid, early, old.
Default prefix
"masterpiece, best quality, newest, absurdres, highres, safe,". Some merges add "very aesthetic, amazing quality, year 2024, very awa".
Default negative
"nsfw, worst quality, old, early, low quality, lowres, signature, username, logo, bad hands, mutated hands, mammal, anthro, furry, ambiguous form, feral, semi-anthro". The e621 words keep furry styles out.
Rating
safe in the prompt and nsfw in the negative by default. Adult work flips them (see Adult (NSFW) packs). Other levels: sensitive, explicit.
Settings (v-pred)
Euler only ("other samplers will not work properly"), CFG 4 to 5, 28 to 35 steps, about 1 MP. A v-pred checkpoint needs v-prediction sampling (ModelSamplingDiscrete set to v_prediction with zsnr) unless the loader sets it.
Mistakes
Asking for a retro look (year 2005) while the negative holds "old, early"; animal words pulling anthro styles; Pony score tags.
For your pack:
- Model Info names it noobai when "noob" is in the file name. The variant rule sits above Illustrious because NoobAI files often mention both.
- Put the prefix in the noobai branch of the model header, and the default negative as that branch's Add to negative.
- If an era wildcard rolls date tags, take "old, early" out of the negative, or the two cancel.
- For real animals, add "no humans, animal focus" and keep the e621 words in the negative.

sections.title: Flux.1 and Flux.2
sections.text:
Black Forest Labs' models read full sentences. Flux.1 dev and schnell use CLIP-L plus T5-XXL and are guidance-distilled, so they run at CFG 1. Flux.2 (Dev and Klein) uses a Mistral-family text encoder.
Prompt form
Full sentences, not tag lists. BFL's frame is Subject, Action, Style, Context (setting, light, time, mood). The model pays more attention to early words, so the subject goes first. 30 to 80 words suits most scenes.
Negative
None. At CFG 1 the negative has no effect; wire an empty encode or ConditioningZeroOut. Say what you want instead ("an empty street"). If you need a real negative, the built-in NAGuidance node restores it.
Weights
Flux.1 parses "(word:1.2)" but the effect is weak; rephrase ("a vivid red dress, the brightest thing in the frame"). Flux.2 turns weights off, so the brackets reach the model as text.
Text in the image
In double quotes, short: a sign that reads "OPEN LATE".
Two boxes
CLIPTextEncodeFlux has clip_l and t5xxl boxes. The same text in both is fine; some put a short tag summary in clip_l.
Flux.2 extras
Hex colours tied to an object work ("a #1E90FF umbrella"). Structured JSON prompts are supported; the field names in community guides are conventions, not a fixed schema.
Mistakes
Tag soup; weight stacks; negative boxes that do nothing; "masterpiece, 8k" (mostly ignored); "beautiful, perfect" instead of describing light and texture, which gives the plastic-skin look.
Adult content
Base Flux.1 lacks explicit anatomy. It is a poor default for an explicit pack.
For your pack:
- Write options as phrases ("a weathered leather jacket"), not tags, and join them with a combine into sentences.
- A prose skeleton: "$subject, $action. $outfit. $place, $light. $camera, $style."
- Option negatives and $negatives do nothing here. Put exclusions into positive wording and constraints.
- Keep weights out of option text for Flux.2.
- A Flux.2 JSON prompt can be a combine that writes the object from variables. Keep the keys stable and keep "|" out of it, since {a|b} is inline-pick syntax.
- Model Info reads both Flux.1 and Flux.2 as flux. Use $model_variant (a rule on the file name) to tell them apart.

sections.title: Z-Image (Turbo and Base)
sections.text:
Alibaba Tongyi's model with a Qwen3-4B text encoder (loaded with the Lumina2 clip type in ComfyUI). Turbo is the popular one: about 9 steps, and no real CFG.
Prompt form
Long, detailed natural language works best. It renders text well; quote it.
Turbo
Official guidance is 0; ComfyUI users run CFG 1 to 2. The negative does nothing.
Base
CFG 3 to 5, and negatives work.
Weights
Off. "(word:1.2)" reaches the model as literal text. Write emphasis in words.
Mistakes
Tag lists; weight brackets; relying on a negative on Turbo.
For your pack:
- Long rolled phrases are fine here, so recipe wildcards with several @{} parts suit it.
- On Turbo, say "a clean plain background" or "plain clothing" in the prompt, or use a constraint, instead of a negative.
- Model Info may read it as lumina2 or under its own class name. Check the Model Info node's output once and pin the variant.

sections.title: Qwen-Image and Qwen-Image 2.1
sections.text:
Alibaba's models use a Qwen vision-language encoder. ComfyUI wraps your prompt in a system line: "Describe the image by detailing the color, shape, size, texture, quantity, text, spatial relationships of the objects and background". That line is a good hint at the order it wants. Qwen-Image 2.1 (2026-09-20, about 7B) is one model for generation and editing, takes up to 10 reference images and outputs 2K.
Prompt form
Sentences, under 200 words. The style can lead ("Art poster design: ..."), then the subject, background, palette and finish. Spatial wording works: "on the left ..., on the right ..., facing each other".
Text
Its strength, including Chinese and Japanese. Quote the text, give its position and style, and never translate it.
Suffix
The official examples end with ", Ultra HD, 4K, cinematic composition."
Negative
The default is a single space. It works at true CFG above 1 (the official setting is true_cfg 4, 50 steps). Lightning setups at CFG 1 ignore it.
Weights
Off: brackets reach the model as text.
Editing
Say what to change and what to keep: "change the jacket to red leather, keep the face, pose and background". In 2.1 a transparency (RGBA) cue gives cut-outs.
Licence
2.1 is under a research licence. Check the card before commercial use.
For your pack:
- A prose skeleton with the caption in quotes: $style: $subject wearing $outfit, $place. A sign reads "$caption". $light.
- Keep the suffix as a fixed value, so a model header can drop it for other families.
- For edit workflows, a wildcard fills the "change" slot and the "keep" part is fixed text in the template.
- Model Info reads Qwen-Image as qwen_image. Check 2.1 once on the node and pin the variant if it reads differently.

sections.title: Anima
sections.text:
A 2B anime model by CircleStone Labs with Comfy Org, built on NVIDIA Cosmos-Predict2, with a Qwen3 0.6B text encoder and the Qwen-Image VAE (about 7 GB of VRAM). Base v1.0 came out on 2026-05-15; Turbo and Aesthetic v1.0 in July 2026.
Prompt form
Tags and sentences mixed, in any order. Write at least two sentences. Name the character first, then describe them.
Prefix
The base is not aesthetic-tuned, so start with "masterpiece, best quality, score_7, safe," and change the rating tag as needed. Score tags use underscores, like Pony V7.
Negative
"worst quality, low quality, score_1, score_2, score_3, artist name".
Base settings
CFG 4 to 5, 30 to 50 steps, the er_sde sampler.
Turbo settings
CFG 1 (the negative is ignored), 8 to 12 steps.
Weak spots
Photorealism and long text in the image.
Licence
Non-commercial. Check the card before you share or sell output.
For your pack:
- The model header's anima branch writes the prefix. The rating word comes from $rating, not typed into the prefix.
- Options can be tags; the template can add a sentence of context around them.
- Model Info probably reads it as cosmos. Pin the variant to anima, or add a rule matching "anima" in the file name.
- On Turbo, the safe guard and every exclusion must be positive wording or constraints.

sections.title: Wan 2.2 (video)
sections.text:
Wan uses a umT5-XXL encoder with room for 512 tokens. A video prompt needs things an image prompt never has: motion, a camera move, and a negative against stillness.
Prompt form
Prose, 80 to 100 words. Simple, direct verbs. One clear action per clip; several moves muddy the result.
Order
Style or medium, subject, appearance and outfit, expression, pose and motion, background, texture, then shot size and angle, then the camera move.
Camera
One move per clip: slow push-in, pan left, tracking shot, orbit, crane up, handheld. Say "static camera" when you want none.
Negative
The official default is a long Chinese list that fights garish colour, overexposure and, unlike any image negative, stillness ("static", "motionless"). Copy it as is. 4 to 8 step accelerated setups run CFG 1 and ignore it.
Image to video
The image already supplies the look. Prompt the motion, not the appearance: subject action, then one camera move, then pace.
Language
The first-last-frame model was trained mainly on Chinese pairs, so Chinese prompts are recommended there.
For your pack:
- Add an $action wildcard and a $camera_move wildcard that image packs don't have.
- Hold $character across a Loop run and let $action and $camera_move roll per clip, so each frame is one shot of a shot list.
- Keep the official negative in a fixed value, and only count on it at CFG above 1.
- Model Info reads it as wan.

sections.title: SDXL base and realistic SDXL fine-tunes
sections.text:
Two CLIP encoders, 75-token chunks, about 1 MP sizes (1024×1024, 832×1216, 1216×832).
Prompt form
Short natural sentences plus style keywords. Keep the subject in the first chunk.
Order
Subject and action, appearance, setting, light, camera, style.
Negative
Short: "lowres, blurry, watermark, text, deformed". Don't paste a whole SD 1.5 negative.
Two boxes
CLIPTextEncodeSDXL has text_g and text_l. Use the same text in both; the labels differ between tools, so don't rely on a style box and a content box.
For your pack: Phrase options ("a linen summer dress") work on both realistic fine-tunes and base. Base SDXL is weak at explicit anatomy; adult work happens on fine-tunes.

sections.title: SD 1.5
sections.text:
One CLIP encoder, 512 px native. Most real use is through fine-tunes: anime ones trained on Danbooru tags, photo ones on captions.
Prompt form
Comma-separated keyword phrases: subject, medium, style, details, colour, light. You don't need every kind.
Negative
Benefits most from a standing negative ("lowres, bad anatomy, bad hands, extra digits, worst quality, low quality, jpeg artifacts, watermark, signature, text") or a negative embedding such as EasyNegative.
Settings
512×512 or 512×768, then hires fix. Anime fine-tunes use clip skip 2.
Mistakes
"trending on artstation, 8k, octane render" filler eating the short window; more than one subject; sizes far from 512.
For your pack: Keep option text short; the whole prompt should fit one or two chunks. A negative embedding goes in the standing negative or an option's negative, so it follows usage.

sections.title: Krea 2
sections.text:
A 12.9B model with Raw and 8-step Turbo versions, released 2026-06-22 and native in ComfyUI. No official prompting guide was found, so this is inferred.
Prompt form
Treat it as a natural-language model: Flux-style sentences.
Negative
Test it. Assume the Turbo version ignores it.
For your pack: Build it like a Flux pack. Model Info has no rule for it yet, so check what the node reads and pin the variant. Revisit this section as guides appear.

sections.title: LTX-2.x (video)
sections.text:
Lightricks' video models (2.3 and 2.5 are among the most opened ComfyUI templates). No primary prompting source was checked for this guide, so this follows the Wan rules.
Prompt form
Prose that states the motion and one camera move, as for Wan.
Negative
Check the template's CFG. Distilled setups at CFG 1 ignore it.
For your pack: Use the same $action and $camera_move slots as a Wan pack. Model Info reads it as ltxv.

sections.title: Chroma
sections.text:
An 8.9B model derived from Flux schnell, using only T5-XXL. It is de-distilled, so it runs with real CFG.
Prompt form
Long natural-language descriptions; a short tag tail also works ("cold color palette, muted colors, detailed").
Negative
Works: "low quality, blurry, deformed, ugly" plus per-concept words. The card's example runs guidance 3 and 40 steps.
Adult content
Reported to be trained without a safety filter. Check the card.
For your pack: Write it like Flux, but option negatives and $negatives do work here. Model Info reads it as chroma.

sections.title: Other families
sections.text:
Family | Prompt | Negative | Notes
SD 3.5 Large / Medium | Sentences; composition terms (bird's eye view, close-up, wide-angle shot); text in double quotes, short | Start with none, add 5 to 15 words when a defect shows; Large Turbo has none | Medium: CFG 3.5 to 7, 28 to 40 steps. Large Turbo: 4 steps, guidance 0 to 1. Filtered base, little explicit capability
HiDream-I1 (Full, Dev, Fast) | Sentences, front-loaded; about 128 tokens, the tail is lost | Full only | Full: CFG about 5, 50 steps. Dev and Fast are distilled: CFG 1
Animagine XL 3.1 | Tags: count, character, series, then the rest; prefix "masterpiece, best quality, very aesthetic, absurdres" | Its default holds "oldest, early", which fights year tags | Rating words safe, sensitive, nsfw, "explicit, nsfw". Model Info variant animagine
Animagine XL 4.0 | Tags: count, character, series, rating, the rest, then quality LAST ("masterpiece, high score, great score, absurdres") | "lowres, bad anatomy, bad hands, worst quality, low score, ..." | CFG 4 to 7 (5), 25 to 28 steps, Euler a. The one popular tag model with quality at the end
Kolors | Chinese or English sentences (ChatGLM3 encoder) | Yes | Guidance about 5 to 6.5, 25 steps
Neta Lumina / NetaYume | Needs a system prompt (Danbooru, natural-language or structured variant); later NetaYume data is tags only | Yes | res_multistep, linear_quadratic, 30+ steps, CFG 4 to 5.5. Keep the system prompt in the Templates library
HunyuanImage 2.1 | Concise sentences; a refiner stage and a prompt enhancer | For artefacts |
Playground v2.5 | SDXL-like sentences and keywords | Yes | Guidance about 3
PixArt, Stable Cascade | SDXL-era prompting, untested | Untested | No data found
HunyuanVideo | Sentences in its encoder's order: theme and subject, attributes and positions, actions and motion, background, light, style, then camera angle and moves | Short artefact list | One clear action per clip
For your pack: for any family not listed, start from its model card's example prompts, copy their order into an Assembler template, and save it in the Templates library. Fixed strings a model needs (a system prompt, a suffix) are fixed values or templates, never wildcards.

sections.title: Section order per family
sections.text:
Family | Dialect | Order | Quality tags
SD 1.5 (base and photo) | keywords | count, character, appearance, outfit, pose, expression, setting, light, camera, style, quality | end
SD 1.5 anime fine-tunes | tags | quality, count, character, appearance, outfit, pose, expression, setting, light, camera, style | start
SDXL base | short sentences | subject and action, appearance, outfit, expression, setting, light, camera, style | optional, end
Pony V6 | tags | score string, source, rating, count, character, appearance, outfit, pose, expression, setting, light, camera, style | start, full string
Pony V7 | sentences plus tags | special tags, plain description, style, extra tags | start (weak)
Illustrious | tags | quality, count, character, artist, appearance, outfit, pose, expression, setting, light, camera, style | start
NoobAI | tags | quality and date prefix, count, character, series, artist, general tags, other | start
Animagine 4.0 | tags | count, character, series, rating, everything else, quality | END
Anima | tags and sentences | prefix with score and rating, character, then description | start
Flux.1, Flux.2, Krea 2, Chroma | sentences | subject, action, style, context (setting, light, camera); quoted text | none
Qwen-Image | sentences | style (may lead), subject, appearance, outfit, pose, positions, setting, palette and light, camera, quoted text, suffix | suffix
Z-Image | long sentences | subject first, then the scene in detail | none
Wan 2.2, LTX | sentences | style, subject, appearance, expression, motion, background, shot, camera move | none
One slot order serves every family. Only the head and the tail change, and the sentence families join the slots into clauses instead of a tag list:
# | Slot | Notes
Head | Quality or score tags, source, rating | Family adapter: a fixed value or the model header derivation
1 | Count and framing | 1girl, solo or "a woman"
2 | Identity | Named character and series, or an original character's fixed traits
3 | Appearance | Face, eyes, hair, skin, body, an adult marker
4 | Outfit | One coherent outfit, or a clothing state
5 | Pose or action | Plus motion for video
6 | Expression and gaze |
7 | Setting | Plus props
8 | Light, time, weather |
9 | Camera and framing | Plus the camera move for video
10 | Style, medium, artist |
Tail | Quality last (Animagine 4.0), the Qwen-Image suffix | Family adapter
For your pack: make one variable per slot, in this order, and write one Assembler template per dialect (one tag skeleton, one prose skeleton). Save both in the Templates library. The head and tail come from the model header (see Recommended pack structure), driven by WP Model Info.

sections.title: What WP Model Info reports
sections.text:
WP Model Info writes $model_family from the model's class and $model_variant from rules on the file name. The family list was written before some newer models, so check what the node reads for yours once:
Model | $model_family | $model_variant
SDXL and its fine-tunes | sdxl | noobai, pony, illustrious or animagine from the file name; others empty
SD 1.5 | sd15 |
SD 3.5 | sd3 |
Flux.1 and Flux.2 | flux (both) | Add a rule to tell them apart
Chroma | chroma |
Pony V7 | auraflow |
HiDream | hidream |
Qwen-Image | qwen_image | Check 2.1 once
Z-Image | probably lumina2 | Check once and pin
Anima | probably cosmos | Pin, or add a rule for "anima"
Wan, LTX, HunyuanVideo | wan, ltxv, hunyuan_video |
Krea 2, Kolors, HunyuanImage 2.1 | the model's class name in snake_case | Check once and pin
For your pack: drive the header from $model_variant where you can, with $model_family as the fallback. A merge without "noob", "pony" or "illustrious" in its file name is not detected: rename it, add a rule, or pin the variant on the node.

sections.title: Subjects
sections.text:
Subject | What to name, in order | In your pack
Portraits (realistic) | Framing first (close-up, head and shoulders, half-body), then identity with an adult age ("a woman in her 30s"), skin texture, one outfit, expression and gaze, the light setup, then lens and aperture | Constrain outfit by framing: no shoes in a close-up. "looking at viewer" is a very strong default; vary it on purpose
Anime characters | Count tag first; character plus series tag; for an original character, a fixed bundle of hair colour, length, style, eye colour and one accessory | Hold the identity bundle across a run. Matching canon traits help; contradicting them fights the character
Several characters | A count tag and clearly different traits each; on sentence models "on the left ..., on the right ..." | Two bundle copies with renamed variables; for a strong split, one Assembler per region. Never draw two people's outfits from one shared pick
Fashion | One named outfit, or up to 3 or 4 layers from the base outward, one colour each, accessories last; say open or closed for outerwear | Constraints for season, formality and era. One top and one bottom, or one piece. Footwear only when the frame shows legs
Landscapes | Foreground, midground, background, sky; time of day and weather are the strongest mood levers; wide lens for vast scenes, telephoto for stacked ridges | On anime tag models add no humans, scenery, or a person appears. One season per image
Architecture | Style, city, hour; two-point perspective or "vertical lines straight"; named materials (board-formed concrete, weathered copper) | "tilt-shift" gives the toy-miniature look. Negative people, cars, text for clean renders
Interiors | Room, style, materials, palette, light, mood; wide angle at eye level | A material wildcard tagged by style, and a Style → Material constraint
Animals | Species, breed, coat, age (puppy or adult), action, setting; wildlife framing (telephoto, eye level) | On Pony and NoobAI, animal words can pull anthro styles: add no humans, animal focus and keep the furry words in the negative
Food | Dish, plating, garnish, surface and props, light direction, palette, angle (45-degree or overhead flat lay) | Name light by direction and colour temperature ("window light from the side", "warm 3200K tungsten")
Products | Product, material, surface, light setup (softbox, rim), background, lens (macro, 85mm) | Keep brand names and trademarks out. Quoted label text on text-capable models only
Photography vocabulary | Shot size, angle, lens (35, 50, 85, 135 mm, macro), aperture and depth of field, light setup (Rembrandt, butterfly, rim, softbox), film stock | Make lens and light their own wildcards and let a Shot → Lens constraint pair them
Sci-fi and fantasy | One or two strong world nouns, then specifics; one material language for armour | Don't stack genres ("steampunk cyberpunk solarpunk"). Keep real nouns and invented nouns in separate vocabularies
Pixel art | "pixel art style", a pixel-art LoRA at 0.6 to 0.8, about 128 px, then a nearest-neighbour downscale | Keep option text short; fine detail words get lost
Manga and comics | monochrome, greyscale, screentone, spot colour, 4koma for strips | A fixed value for the manga look plus an exclude constraint against colour wildcards
Vehicles | Make or type, era, colour and finish, angle (three-quarter front), setting, motion blur | An Era → Setting constraint
Abstract, patterns, textures | Medium, palette, motif, symmetry; "seamless tile" for patterns | No subject wildcard at all
Logos and icons | Flat, vector, limited palette, centred, plain background | Text-capable models only; quote any text
Creatures | Body plan, skin, features, a scale reference, habitat | A Habitat → Body plan constraint keeps them believable
Mecha and hardware | Frame type, armour style, weapons, markings, pose, setting | Tag models know mecha, science fiction
Horror | Atmosphere (fog, low key), subject, setting, palette | Gore is an adult register: label the pack nsfw and gate it behind a $rating driver
Concept art | "concept art, matte painting", composition terms (establishing shot), mood | Sentences on prose models
Children's book illustration | An art style, not a subject age: watercolour or gouache, soft palette, simple shapes; animal or adult characters by default | Never mix it with adult vocabulary. Add a hard exclude constraint from this style to any adult register
Historical | Era, region, clothing by era, architecture | An Era → Clothing constraint. No named real people
Cosplay | "cosplay" plus the character name, adult anchors | No real cosplayers or other real people by name or likeness
Typography | The text in quotes, then font style, placement and background | "$caption" in a template works. Keep captions short: long rolled text turns to gibberish on SDXL-family models. Qwen is strong for CJK
For your pack: the subject decides which slots exist. A landscape pack has no outfit slot; a product pack has no expression. Build only the slots the subject needs and constrain the ones that depend on framing.

sections.title: Prompt types beyond text to image
sections.text:
Type | How to prompt | With Wildcard Pipeline
img2img | Describe the target image, not the change. Denoise 0.3 to 0.5 keeps the composition; 0.6 to 0.8 restyles | Roll style and light; keep the subject in fixed values or held picks
Inpainting | Start near denoise 0.5. With "only masked", describe only what goes in the mask, but keep the full image's style tags so it blends. Inpaint checkpoints take higher denoise | WP Image Filter: paint a mask and edit the prompt in the picker; the edited prompt is re-encoded when its clip input is wired
Outpainting | Keep at least 20% overlap. Describe the new scene and background, not the subject again. Flux Fill runs at denoise 1 | A second Assembler that renders only $place, $light and $style
Hires fix (two passes) | Same prompt as the first pass, denoise 0.3 to 0.5 (up to 0.6), latent upscale at most 2× | WP Var → Bool on a $hires variable switches it per pick; WP Image Filter can gate it on your pick
ADetailer and FaceDetailer | A blank detailer prompt uses the main one. [SEP] gives one prompt per detected object, in no fixed order; [SKIP] skips one; [PROMPT] inserts the main prompt | Feed it from a second Assembler that renders only face and expression variables. With several people the order can swap, so prefer one shared face prompt. In adult packs it must carry the adult anchors
ControlNet | Start at weight 0.5 to 0.7; pick balanced or "my prompt is more important" | The pose comes from the control image: hide $pose, or switch it off with a derivation on an injected $controlnet value
IP-Adapter and style transfer | Pick the style transfer or precise weight type; the text should still name the subject. Face models mostly ignore text: CFG 3 to 4 | With a style reference, hide the $style wildcard so text and image don't fight
Regional prompting | A base prompt plus one prompt per region (Set Area or Set Mask with Combine; FluxRegionAttention for Flux) | One Assembler per region, all reading the same Context, so the picks agree
LoRA triggers and stacking | Take the trigger from the model page. Start at 0.7 to 0.8; stack 2 or 3 at 0.4 to 0.8, under about 2 in total; the base family must match | Put the trigger in the wildcard option that is the LoRA, so pick and trigger travel together. WP Var → Float can feed the strength. Never blocklist or fuzzy-dedupe trigger words in the Cleaner
Embeddings | embedding:name in the text, optionally weighted; they only work on the family they were trained for | Negative embeddings go in an option's negative, so they follow usage
Video (Wan i2v) | Prompt the motion: subject action, one camera move, pace. "static camera" for none | Hold $character; roll $action and $camera_move per frame
For your pack: second passes usually want a smaller prompt than the first. A second WP Prompt Assembler reading the same Context renders just the slots that pass needs, and its picks match the first pass because they come from the same run.

sections.title: Variation without incoherence
sections.text:
Each slot that varies on its own multiplies the chance of a bad combination. A good budget is 2 to 4 varying slots per image (say pose, expression, camera and one prop), with everything else fixed or held.
- Fixed for a whole set: the family head, the subject count, the character's identity (face, hair, eyes, body, the adult marker), the style.
- Fixed within a scene: the outfit, the setting, the light.
- Varies per image or frame: pose, expression, camera, small props.
- Vary inside a slot with curated options of one kind (ten poses that all fit the framing), not mixed lists.
- A fixed seed doesn't keep a character the same once the prompt changes. Hold the picks instead.
For your pack: use Hold across run for identity and style under a WP Context Loop, weights for how often each option shows, constraints to forbid bad pairs and a fallback for when a constraint leaves nothing.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.text:
Mistake | Symptom | Fix
Contradicting tags (smile and crying, nude and jacket, from behind and looking at viewer) | A muddled, random result | Constrain or derive the slots that depend on each other
Tag soup (60+ tags, many colours) | Colour leak; tags past the second chunk ignored | About 40 tags at most, 3 colours at most, colours next to their nouns
Duplicates | Uncontrolled emphasis | WP Prompt Cleaner after the Assembler (the Assembler never dedupes)
Too many subjects | One vanishes or two fuse | Two at most without regional tools
Another family's special tags | Wasted tokens, odd style | A model header per family
Weight brackets on Qwen, Z-Image or Flux.2 | Literal "(…:1.2)" in the prompt | Write emphasis in words
Negatives on CFG 1 models | Nothing happens | Positive wording, constraints, or NAG
A huge generic negative | Cancels things you asked for | A short standing negative plus option negatives
No count tag | Extra people | 1girl, solo or "a single woman" first
Detail the frame can't show (shoes in a portrait) | Changed crops, colour bleed | Constrain outfit and pose by framing
A video prompt without motion or camera | A static clip | Motion and camera-move slots
Pony's score string cut to score_9 | Weak quality | The full string
For your pack: run the Test Runner over many seeds and read a handful of full prompts. Most of these mistakes are visible in the text before you render a single image.

pages.title: Adult (NSFW) packs
pages.blurb: Structure, tag norms and the safeguards every adult pack must carry.

sections.title: Safeguards
sections.text:
One rule is enforced: the AI assistant never writes a minor in a sexual context. The rest of this list is our strong recommendation for any pack that can reach suggestive or explicit content. Your own edits are never checked or changed.
No minors, ever
Never make sexual or suggestive content of minors or of characters presented as minors, in any form, and never loli or shota content. This holds whatever the request, whatever a canon age claim says ("she's really 1000 years old") and whatever the art style.
Adult anchors
Every character in a pack that can reach suggestive or explicit carries a positive adult anchor: "mature female" or "mature male" plus adult body descriptors on tag models, "an adult woman in her 30s" on sentence models. Use ages of 25 and up where a model reads ages.
Youth negative block
Every such render carries the youth block in its standing negative: "child, loli, shota, toddler, aged down, young" on tag models, "child, minor, teenager, young girl, young boy, childlike" on sentence models.
No youth-coded content
School uniforms, school settings, childlike props and age numbers under 18 are safe-only options. Never pair petite or small body descriptors with youth-coded tags or a "cute, small" style. Named characters whose canon age is under 18 stay out of adult registers, even drawn "aged up".
No real people
No real person's name, likeness or lookalike description, including real cosplayers.
Blocklist backstop
A WP Prompt Cleaner blocklist after the Assembler catches what slips through. It matches whole words, so list every variant (below).
The safeguards work in layers, and no single layer is enough: constraints keep youth-coded options out of adult registers at the source, the adult anchor steers every character in the prompt, the youth block pushes away in the negative (at CFG above 1), and the blocklist removes what slipped through.
What the assistant does. In every AI feature (chat, Draft with AI, the Pack builder), an option, value, rule or template that puts a clearly minor word (child, loli, shota, an age under 18) next to a sexual or nude one is left out. In a Pack builder pack rated NSFW, the whole pack counts as that context, so a clearly minor word is left out wherever it is. Words an adult can wear or be called too (school uniform, teen, younger sister) are kept, with a Check warning on the item so you can judge them. Settings › Youth negative (on by default) adds the youth block to the template's negative; turn it off to write your own.
For your pack: build the safeguards first, before any content. They are a few fixed values, one negative template and one Cleaner node.

sections.title: Register is a variable, not a label
sections.text:
The library's content rating (safe or nsfw) is a label for lists and publishing. It changes nothing in a run. What decides how explicit an image gets is a hidden rating driver: one wildcard, picked once, that every adult slot is constrained by. The same driver picks the model's rating tag, so the tag and the content never disagree.
- To cap a node at safe or suggestive, untick the higher levels on that use of the Rating wildcard. Nothing downstream can reach them then.
- For one model family, a Rating tag wildcard plus a diagonal Only constraint maps the level to the right word. For a pack that serves several families, a derivation with AND conditions on $model_variant and $_rating writes it instead.
- On a mixed model, the safe level also needs a guard: Pony's rating_safe in the prompt and rating_explicit in the negative; NoobAI's and Anima's safe prefix word. On CFG 1 models the guard must be positive wording.
For your pack: one rating driver per pack, first in the stack, hidden. Never roll the rating tag on its own.

sections.title: Blueprint: rating-aware adult pack
sections.text:
Modules in running order, for a Danbooru-tag model:
# | Module | Kind | Writes | Options and settings
1 | Rating | Wildcard | $_rating | safe (fallback), suggestive, explicit. Hide from prompt. Untick the levels a node must never reach
2 | Rating → Rating tag | Constraint | | Only on the diagonal: safe → safe, suggestive → suggestive, explicit → explicit
3 | Rating tag | Wildcard | $rating_tag | Your family's words (table below), tagged safe, suggestive, explicit
4 | Character bundle | Bundle | $character, $body, $hair, $eyes | $character starts with the person's count tag (1girl, 1boy). Every option of $body carries the adult anchor (mature female, curvy, mature male, muscular). Hold across run
5 | Rating → Clothing state | Constraint | | Matrix with Only cells: safe allows fully clothed; suggestive adds revealing and underwear; explicit allows the whole ladder
6 | Clothing state | Wildcard | $clothing_state | The ladder below, each option tagged with its register and with what it needs (top, bottom, none). Option negatives by state
7 | Clothing state → Outfit | Constraint | | topless → Only bottoms; bottomless → Only tops; underwear only → Only underwear; nude → Only the outfit's null option
8 | Outfit | Wildcard | $outfit | Tagged top, bottom, one piece, underwear. A null option. School uniforms tagged safe only, and excluded from the other registers
9 | Rating → Pose | Constraint | | Only the poses tagged for that register
10 | Pose | Wildcard | $pose | Tagged by register and by framing
11 | Pose → Camera | Constraint | | Framing that fits the pose ("on back" with "from above"; "from behind" without face detail)
12 | Camera | Wildcard | $camera | Framing tags: portrait, upper body, cowboy shot, full body
13 | Rating → Act | Constraint | | safe and suggestive: Only the act's null option
14 | Act | Wildcard | $act | Explicit only. One act per option, each starting with the partner's count tag and the pairing tag (1boy, hetero, ...), so the counts never disagree with the act
15 | Solo when alone | Derivation | $count | IF $act has no value (NOT with "has value") → solo
16 | Clothing state → Place | Constraint | | Undressed states boost private places (bedroom, onsen, shower); public places with nudity only as a deliberate theme
17 | Censorship | Fixed values | $censor | uncensored with negative censored, mosaic censoring, bar censor, or the reverse. Switch it by hand; never roll it
Template: $quality, $rating_tag, $character, $count, $act, $body, $hair, $eyes, $clothing_state, $outfit, $pose, $expression, $place, $camera, $censor, $styleNegative template: $negatives, child, loli, shota, toddler, aged down, young, bad anatomy, extra arms, extra legs, extra fingers, watermark
- The count tags come first: the character's own, then solo or the partner's from the act. Below explicit the act is empty, so the derivation writes solo.
- An Only rule pointing at a null option is how a constraint says "nothing here": for a nude state the outfit prints nothing, and below explicit the act prints nothing.
- On a sentence model, keep the same modules and write the options as phrases. A combine builds each person's sentence with the adult anchor in it.
- For two adults, insert the character bundle twice with the second copy's variables renamed, give each an anchor, and hold both. Regional prompting or one Assembler per person keeps their traits apart.

sections.title: The clothing-state ladder
sections.text:
A graded wildcard of clothing states, tagged by the registers that may use each and by what each needs from the outfit:
State | Registers | Outfit allowed | Option negative
fully clothed | safe, suggestive, explicit | top and bottom, or one piece | nude, nipples (in a suggestive register)
revealing clothes | suggestive, explicit | top and bottom, or one piece | nude
open shirt, shirt lift, clothes pull, clothing aside | explicit | the garment the state acts on (a shirt for open shirt, a skirt for skirt lift) |
topless | explicit | bottoms only | bra, shirt
bottomless | explicit | tops only | skirt, pants, panties
underwear only, lingerie | suggestive, explicit | underwear only | dress, shirt, pants
nude, completely nude | explicit | no garments (accessories only if the template says so) | clothes, underwear, panties, bra
For your pack: the state is a decision (constraints read it), so it is its own wildcard. Its option negatives follow usage, so each state pushes away exactly the garments it rules out. Under a Loop, a planned sequence can step along the ladder with per-frame overrides or a Frame wildcard and a constraint, while the character and outfit stay held.

sections.title: Coherence rules
sections.text:
- One clothing state per character, picked first. Everything else follows it: the outfit only draws garments the state allows, and "open shirt" needs a shirt, "skirt lift" a skirt.
- The negative follows the state: nude puts clothes in the negative, topless puts a bra and shirt there, fully clothed in a suggestive register puts nudity there. This is the best use of option negatives in an adult pack.
- Pose decides framing and what is visible. Constrain the camera by the pose rather than rolling them apart. Framing is also the main lever for keeping explicit detail where you want it.
- One act per image, with the people counted: "1girl, 1boy, hetero" for a couple, "2girls, yuri", "solo" for one person. Several acts at once fuse bodies.
- Body description is identity, not variety. Hold it across a run. In adult packs it also carries the adult anchor, so it is never optional.
- The expression fits the act and register. Avoid pairs that fight (smile and crying) unless you mean it.
- Standing anatomy negatives: "bad anatomy, extra arms, extra legs, extra fingers, fused fingers, missing limbs, deformed". Add "extra people" when the count is small.
- The rating tag must agree with the content. rating_safe with nude fights itself; rating_explicit on a clothed café scene drifts toward nudity. That is why the rating tag comes from the same driver as the slots.
For your pack: every rule here is a constraint between two wildcards, or an option negative. Write the rule once and the pack keeps it on every seed.

sections.title: Rating tags by model family
sections.text:
Danbooru rates every post general, sensitive, questionable or explicit. Each model family maps those four levels to its own words:
Family | Rating words | Notes
Pony V6 | rating_safe, rating_questionable, rating_explicit, after the score and source tags | Trained on equal thirds of each rating. For safe output on a mixed merge: rating_safe in the prompt and rating_explicit in the negative
Pony V7 | rating_* special tags | Much weaker than V6's special tags; lean on the description
Illustrious | Danbooru's levels: general, sensitive, questionable, explicit, or the merge's own form (nsfw, rating:explicit) | Read the merge's page
NoobAI | safe, sensitive, nsfw, explicit | The default prefix has safe and the default negative has nsfw. For adult work swap the prefix word and take nsfw out of the negative
Animagine 3.1 / 4.0 | safe, sensitive, nsfw, explicit, nsfw | 4.0 puts the rating right after the series
Anima | safe in the default prefix; the same four levels as NoobAI | Turbo runs at CFG 1, so the negative is ignored. Non-commercial licence
Chroma | Plain description | Reported to be trained without a safety filter; real negatives work
SDXL base, SD 3.5, Flux.1, Qwen-Image, Z-Image | None | Weak or absent explicit anatomy. Adult work needs a fine-tune or LoRA; Flux is a poor default
Realistic merges | The merge's own | Follow the merge's page
For your pack: exactly one rating word per prompt, in the family's head (see Writing prompts for your model for where the head goes).

sections.title: Tag vocabulary norms
sections.text:
Use common tags
Danbooru tags with fewer than about 5,000 posts are learned weakly. Prefer the high-count synonym ("nude" over a rare variant).
Clothing state
The ladder above uses real Danbooru tags: open clothes, open shirt, clothes pull, shirt lift, skirt lift, clothing aside, topless, bottomless, underwear only, lingerie, nude, completely nude, naked towel.
Adult body
mature female, mature male, curvy, wide hips, toned, muscular female, abs. These are also the standard steer toward clearly adult depictions on anime models.
Count and pairing
1girl, 1boy, 2girls, solo; hetero, yuri, yaoi. They come first, before the character.
Acts and positions
Danbooru keeps these in its "sexual positions" and "sex acts" tag groups. Draw one per image from a short, curated list, never from a full group dump.
Censorship
About a third of Danbooru's explicit art is censored ("censored" 456K posts against "uncensored" 134K), so Danbooru models add mosaics or bars by default. "uncensored" in the prompt plus "censored, mosaic censoring, bar censor" in the negative turns that off; the reverse turns it on.
Sentence models
Describe plainly and clinically, with the adult anchor in the same sentence as the person ("an adult woman in her 30s, nude, lying on a bed in a dim bedroom").
CFG 1 models
The negative is ignored, so a safe guard must be positive wording ("fully clothed in a buttoned wool coat") plus constraints.
For your pack: curate short lists of well-known tags. A small list of coherent options beats a large one that can contradict itself.

sections.title: Setting up the blocklist
sections.text:
WP Prompt Cleaner's blocklist in list mode matches each entry as a whole word, ignoring case. In tags mode it drops the whole tag that contains the word; in text mode it removes just the word. Because it matches whole words, blocking child does not touch children or childlike. List every form:
Entry | Also list
child | children, childlike, childish, child's
kid | kids, kiddo
loli | lolis, lolicon
shota | shotas, shotacon
toddler | toddlers
minor | minors (this also removes "minor" in other senses)
underage |
teen | teens, teenage, teenager, teenagers, preteen
schoolgirl | schoolgirls, schoolboy, schoolboys
young girl | little girl, young boy, little boy
aged down |
Or switch the blocklist to regex mode, one pattern per line, such as \bchild\w*, \bkids?\b, \b(loli|shota)(s|con)?\b, \btoddlers?\b, \b(pre)?teen(s|age|ager|agers)?\b, \bschool ?(girl|boy)s?\b, \b(little|young) (girl|boy)s?\b and \baged down\b.
Don't block young on its own in the positive: it would also cut "young woman" style wording without making anything safer. Keep it in the negative block. When the Cleaner also cleans the negative, leave the blocklist off in its negative column (the default there), or it would remove the youth block.
For your pack: the blocklist is the last layer, not the first. If it ever removes something, fix the option that produced it.

sections.title: Second passes and edits
sections.text:
- ADetailer and FaceDetailer reuse the main prompt when their prompt is blank. A custom detailer prompt must carry the adult anchors.
- An inpaint edit, or a prompt edited in WP Image Filter's picker, is a new prompt. It needs the anchors and, at CFG above 1, the youth block.
- Artistic nude and explicit are different registers. Artistic nude uses photography and fine-art words (light, pose, medium) at the questionable level.
- Horror gore is an adult register too: label it nsfw and gate it behind the rating driver.
For your pack: a second Assembler for the detailer, reading the same Context, renders the face slots plus the anchor variable, so the anchor can't be forgotten.

sections.title: Before you share
sections.text:
- The library's content rating is set to nsfw. It is only a label for lists and publishing, but it tells others what the pack is.
- Every character's identity option carries an adult anchor, and Hold across run keeps it for the whole Loop.
- The youth block is in the Assembler's negative template itself, not only in option negatives, so it is there on every render.
- No option reachable from suggestive or explicit holds a youth term, a school item or a real person. Pin the Rating wildcard to each level in the Test Runner and read the prompts.
- The Cleaner's blocklist lists every variant, and stays off in the Cleaner's negative column (its default there), where it would strip the youth block.
- Detailer, inpaint and Image Filter prompts carry the adult anchors too. A blank ADetailer prompt reuses the main prompt; a custom one or an edited prompt in the picker is a new prompt.
- The pack says it needs CFG above 1 if it relies on negatives.
- The model's licence and the host's rules allow the use. Some models restrict adult or commercial use (Anima's licence is non-commercial).
- No imported tag dumps. Third-party adult wildcard files and raw tag-group files include prohibited categories; curate by hand.
- Non-consent themes and categories that sharing sites ban (incest, self-harm, bodily excretion and similar) are not in the pack.

sections.title: The pipeline
sections.text: When a WP Context runs, it works through its module stack from top to bottom. Each module produces one or more name = value bindings. Those bindings build up inside the Context and are then passed downstream to Assemblers, other Contexts, or Debug nodes. The Assembler's job is to take your prompt template and swap in the values — every $name token becomes the value that was set upstream.

sections.title: Syntax reference
sections.text:
The following constructs are recognised inside template strings and wildcard option text:
Syntax | Where it works | What it does
$name | combine, derivation, assembler | Reads the named variable from the Context and inserts its value. For a multi-pick variable, bare $name joins the whole list with its separator.
$name.K | combine, derivation, assembler | Indexes a single item out of a multi-pick result — K is 0-based, so $colors.0 is the first pick. Out-of-range indices resolve to empty.
$name.AXIS | combine, derivation, assembler | Reads the tag an accepts axis named AXIS rolled on the source wildcard — e.g. $outfit.SHOES is the shoe tag chosen this run. Rolled once when the option is picked, so it's the same value in every template, module and chained node. For a multi-pick source, $name.K.AXIS is the K-th pick's (index and axis compose in either order). A tag that was never promoted to an accepts axis — or one in a classify group — resolves to empty and is flagged.
@{8hexchars} | wildcard options, derivation actions | Nested module reference — resolves to the picked value of the target wildcard. Segments are optional and combinable: #name caches a display name (shown only if the row is missing), :filter narrows a referenced wildcard's pool by a sub-category boolean expression (e.g. warm or cool), and !null drops the null option. Full form: @{abcd1234#Mood:calm or intense!null}. Filter grammar: Chips & references.
{a|b|c} | all text fields | Picks one alternative at render time. Weight an arm with N::value (e.g. {3::cat|dog} makes cat 3× as likely). The Assembler has no seed, so it leaves picks literal.
{N$$sep$$a|b|c} | all text fields | Multi-pick: picks N items joined by sep. Without a separator ({2$$a|b|c}) they are joined by a comma. {N-M$$sep$$…} picks a random count in the N–M range. Default is UNIQUE (no repeats); add ~ ({N~$$…} / {N-M~$$…}) for INDEPENDENT picks with replacement, which may repeat.
$$ · @@ · {{ | all text fields | Escapes — produce a literal $, @, or { instead of starting a token.
An inline pick's arms are resolved recursively, so an arm can itself contain $vars, @{} refs, and further {…} picks — for example {a @{abcd1234} cat|{2$$, $$red|blue|green} sky}. What each nested token resolves to still depends on the surface it sits on — see the gate below.
Variable names must match ^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*$, be at most 64 characters, and must not start with __ (reserved for internal use). Ref UUIDs are exactly 8 lowercase hex characters.

sections.title: The per-surface gate
sections.text:
Not every token resolves on every surface — each module resolves only what makes sense for it; anything else stays literal text. "Dropped" means the token prints nothing and WP Debug notes it.
Surface | $var read | @{uuid} ref | {a|b} pick
Wildcard option value | — | ✓ | ✓
Combine template | ✓ | dropped | ✓
Derivation action value | ✓ | ✓ | ✓
Derivation condition value | — | — | —
Fixed Values value | — | — | ✓
Prompt Assembler template | ✓ | dropped | literal
Wildcards and fixed values are producers — their option text doesn't read $var at all. So a wildcard can't pull in a value another module set, no matter the order. To build a value from earlier picks, add a combine or derivation after the producers — those surfaces do read $var.
The Assembler is seedless: any leftover {a|b} picks in the final template render verbatim and @{} refs print nothing, so roll the value upstream and reference its $var. Derivation action values resolve @{} refs too — a rule can inject a nested wildcard's pick — while a derivation condition tests one variable ($name.K, $name.AXIS and $name.neg included) against plain text: the value it compares to never resolves anything.

sections.text: Figure: Modules produce $vars inside a Context; the Assembler fills the template. Diagram of the variable pipeline. Across the top, labelled modules inside the Context, sit five module kinds: Wildcard, Fixed Values, Combine, Derivation and Constraint, with a down arrow into the flow below. The flow runs left to right: WP Context (rolls + resolves), an arrow labelled emits, a group of resolved $vars chips ($subject, $style, $lighting), an arrow labelled fills, Prompt Assembler (with a template beginning 'A $style portrait…'), an arrow labelled prompt, and CLIP Encode (conditioning). Caption: modules produce $vars inside a Context, and the Assembler fills the template.

pages.title: Chips & references
pages.blurb: The chips in text fields, their three states, @{uuid#name:filter} refs, and the filter grammar.

sections.title: Variables and chips
sections.text:
Text fields that understand pipeline syntax colour what they recognise. Two kinds of token matter here:
- Variables ($mood, $outfit.SHOES) read a variable from the Context. They are ordinary text in their own colour, wherever variables can be read: combine and derivation text and the Prompt Assembler template. You edit them like any other word. Each name keeps the same colour everywhere, so $mood in a combine matches the one in the Assembler's variable strip. Hover one to see which module writes it, or that it binds at runtime.
- Ref chips (@{abcd1234#Mood}) embed a fresh pick from another module. They appear where references work: wildcard options and derivation actions. A chip shows the target's name, not its id, and it is one unit: the caret steps over it in one move and Backspace deletes it whole, so you can't half-delete a reference and leave broken syntax behind.
Under the chip the field still stores plain text. Copying a chip copies its syntax, and pasting that syntax anywhere turns back into the same chip.

sections.title: The three states
sections.text:
Resolved
The chip points at something real. A ref chip is tinted with the colour of the module it points at (violet ✦ for a wildcard) and hovering it shows the target's id and option count.
Filtered
A resolved ref chip that narrows its pool. A funnel icon means it carries a sub-category filter, a ban icon means it excludes the null option. Hover shows the filter as it reads and how many options still match, e.g. "3 of 8 options match". Click the chip to edit the filter.
Broken
A red chip with a ? icon: the reference points at a module id that isn't in your library (a placeholder, a deleted module, or one never imported here). Hover shows the name it carries, when the reference stored one. Click it to point it at another module. The editors also outline the field and mark its row (an option, a derivation branch) in red, so you can find it in a long table. At run time it produces nothing and the run reports an "Unresolved reference" warning.
A variable never turns red in the library just because nothing produces it yet: variables can be set at run time (by an injector, a loop, or a Context further up the chain). Its hover says binds at runtime. On the canvas, where the graph is known, a name nothing upstream writes is red with a wavy underline and its hover says no upstream producer. An accessor like $outfit.SHOES whose axis the wildcard doesn't declare is underlined too, because it would render empty.

sections.title: Inserting variables and chips (and placeholders)
sections.text:
Type $ to open the variable list, or @ to open the module list. Keep typing to narrow the list, then pick with Enter or a click.
Picking a wildcard that has sub-categories (or a null option) opens a second step, the filter picker, where you can type a filter expression and tick Exclude null. Press Enter to insert the chip, or leave the expression empty for an unfiltered reference. You can reopen the same picker later by clicking the chip.
Placeholders. To use a variable nothing produces yet, type $ and the name, e.g. $lighting, then a space or a comma (or press Enter when the list is empty). The name is filled in by whatever module later writes $lighting. Until then it renders empty and the Assembler marks it as missing, which is a handy to-do marker while you build a template ahead of its modules.
Module placeholders. The same works for a module you haven't built yet. Type @ and the name, e.g. @castle. When no module has that name, the last row of the list is Placeholder @castle. Pick it to insert a red broken chip under that name. The row it sits in is marked red too, and the list view shows its warning triangle, so it can't be forgotten. Once the module exists, click the chip and point it at the module.

sections.title: @{uuid#name:filter} versus plain @name
sections.text:
A reference is always written with braces and the target's 8-character id. Typing @name does not make a reference: it stays literal text and goes into the prompt as written. Use the @ list to insert the chip and the editor writes the full form for you. The long form has four segments, and only the id is required:
Segment | Example | What it does
id | @{abcd1234} | The module's 8 lowercase hex characters. This is what the engine resolves, so renaming the target never breaks the reference.
#name | @{abcd1234#Mood} | A remembered label. Only used for display, and to tell you what a broken chip used to point at.
:filter | @{abcd1234#Mood:warm or calm} | Only options whose sub-categories satisfy the expression can be picked. Grammar below.
!null | @{abcd1234#Mood:warm!null} | Drops the wildcard's null option from the pool. Without it, the null option always stays in, whatever the filter says.
Where a plain name is enough, reach for a variable instead: $mood reads the value an upstream wildcard already picked, while @{…} rolls the referenced wildcard again, on the spot, from its (optionally filtered) pool.

sections.title: Filter expression grammar
sections.text:
A filter is plain boolean English over the referenced wildcard's sub-category names. Each option is tested against its own tags, and it stays in the pool when the expression is true.
Write | Keeps options that
warm | carry the warm tag
not warm | don't carry warm (options with no tags at all count)
warm and bright | carry both
warm or cool · warm, cool | carry either (a comma is short for or)
not warm and (low or high) | don't carry warm, and carry low or high
not (warm or cool) | carry neither
- Precedence: not binds tightest, then and, then or. So a or b and c means a or (b and c). Use parentheses whenever you mean something else; they nest to any depth.
- Operators are lowercase words. Symbols like !, & or | are not operators, and ! is reserved for the !null flag. Write not warm, never !warm.
- Tag names match exactly, including case. A name can't contain spaces or any of ( ) ! , # : { } @ $, and and, or, not and null are reserved.
- Null is a flag, not a term. To keep the null option out, tick Exclude null (the !null segment); writing not null in the expression is an error.
The filter picker checks the expression as you type. It shows how the expression reads as (fully parenthesised where it matters), how many options match, and flags an unknown sub-category with a did you mean fix. If a valid filter matches no option, the reference resolves to empty at run time and raises a Sub-category filter matched nothing warning that lists the tags the pool actually has (see Warning & conflict types).

sections.title: The flow
sections.text: Figure: Each Context inherits the upstream map; the last write for any $var wins. Steps: WP Context A (rolls $vars) → feeds → WP Context B (adds / overrides) → merged $vars → Prompt Assembler (fills template). Flow diagram of three nodes left to right: WP Context A (rolls $vars), an arrow labelled feeds, WP Context B (adds / overrides), an arrow labelled merged $vars, and Prompt Assembler (fills template). Caption: each Context inherits the upstream map, and the last write for any $var wins.

sections.title: How chaining works
sections.text:
A WP Context node has an optional upstream input. When you connect one Context into another, the downstream Context starts with all the variables the upstream already produced, then runs its own modules on top. Any variable the downstream modules set replaces the upstream value for that name. Variables that the downstream does not touch pass through unchanged.
This makes it easy to build a base Context (character, setting) and then add a second Context that overrides only $style, leaving everything else alone. You can chain as many Contexts as you like — the last value written for any variable is what the Assembler receives.
Use WP Context Injector for one-off variable overrides without adding a full new Context node — it lets you route any node output into a named $variable slot.
Figure: Two WP Context nodes chained into a Prompt Assembler. The upstream Context publishes Starter subject + Starter style. The downstream Context holds a single Override Style row (OVERRIDE badge) that writes $style again. Last write wins, so the assembler reads the override $style while $subject flows through unchanged, resolving 'A picture of a cat, in the style of minimalist line art'. Screenshot of two chained WP Context nodes feeding a WP Prompt Assembler. The upstream WP Context (modules 2 / 2) holds Starter subject and Starter style, which publishes $style. Its context output goes into the upstream input of the second WP Context (modules 1 / 1), which holds a single wildcard row Override Style marked with an OVERRIDE badge, reading '$style · 2 options'. The assembler's template is 'A picture of a $subject, in the style of $style' with $subject and $style as 2 upstream chips, and the preview resolves to 'A picture of a cat, in the style of minimalist line art'. The point: $subject flows through untouched while the later Context's $style wins (last write wins).

sections.title: Internal variables survive the chain
sections.text: When you mark a variable as internal in a module's settings, it travels through the chain to downstream Contexts and combine/derivation modules — it is only hidden at the very end, when the Assembler renders the final prompt string. This means a variable you need for intermediate calculations can be internal from the start, passing through as many chained Contexts as you like, and it still will not appear in the rendered prompt.

sections.title: Constraint modules cross chain boundaries
sections.text:
A constraint module placed in one Context can still apply to a wildcard in a later Context downstream. You can even create a dedicated "constraints" Context that does nothing but hold constraint modules, and chain it before the Context with the target wildcards — the constraints fire when those wildcards roll, exactly as if they were in the same Context.
Separating constraints into their own Context keeps your module stacks readable when you have complex pairing rules across many wildcards.
